918.title: Guanyin
918.hook: in China, Avalokiteshvara becomes Guanyin, the one who hears the cries of the world
918.howItsDone: Across East Asia, Buddhists call on Guanyin by name, keep her image at home and in temples, and chant the Lotus Sutra's chapter on the bodhisattva, often called the Universal Gate chapter.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ennin's diary of 845, bells melted and robes taken off. Your line: what survived.

A white figure stands on a rock above the sea, or sits on a lotus, a small vase tipped in one hand. She's in temples and taxi cabs, on kitchen shelves and in restaurant corners, in China and well beyond it. Fishermen have called on her in storms. Mothers have called on her at bedsides. Trace her back far enough, past the white robes and the vase, and you arrive at an Indian bodhisattva this path has already met, shown in India as a man, with a long Sanskrit name: Avalokiteshvara.
screen: `A WHITE FIGURE ABOVE THE SEA.` → `CALLED ON IN STORMS.` → `AN INDIAN NAME UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: The Lotus Sutra has a chapter given over to this bodhisattva, and in China it was copied, chanted and carried on its own. In it, the Buddha is asked why the bodhisattva has this name. His answer is the heart of today: when beings in any kind of trouble call the name with one mind, the bodhisattva perceives the sound of their voices, and they are set free. Fire, flood, shipwreck, a raised sword, chains: the chapter goes through them one by one. In Chinese the name became Guanshiyin, shortened to Guanyin, and it carries that scene inside it: the one who perceives the sounds of the world. Not the one who rules it or judges it. The one who hears. The same chapter says the bodhisattva takes whatever form will help the one who is suffering: a monk, a king, a child, a woman. In China, over time, Guanyin came to be pictured more and more as a woman, robed in white, gentle and near. Some Chinese stories give her a human life, like the tale of Princess Miaoshan, who gave her own eyes and arms to heal the father who had rejected her. People who love Guanyin hold both: the Indian bodhisattva of the sutra and the mother figure of the shrine. And a bodhisattva whose whole name is listening says something about compassion. Before it fixes anything, it hears. It turns toward the sound instead of away from it.
screen: `THE LOTUS SUTRA'S CHAPTER.` · `GUANYIN: PERCEIVING THE SOUNDS.` · `WHATEVER FORM WILL HELP.` · `COMPASSION STARTS BY HEARING.` · then, large: `SHE HEARS THE CRIES.`

Guanyin. The Chinese name for Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva who perceives the sounds of the world and answers in whatever form will help.
Your line: she hears the cries. Compassion starts by turning toward the sound. See you tomorrow.

919.title: Korea
919.hook: a monk arrives in a Korean kingdom carrying images and texts, and the teaching takes root
919.howItsDone: Korean Buddhists remember Sundo's arrival in Goguryeo and Ichadon's death in Silla as founding moments, and Ichadon is still honored in Korea as a martyr who opened the way for the teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Guanyin, the bodhisattva whose name is about hearing. Your line: she hears the cries.

A monk arrives at a royal court on a peninsula, and he isn't traveling light. He brings images of the Buddha and written scriptures, a gift from a Chinese ruler to a Korean king. The king could send him back. He could lock the gifts in a treasury and forget them. Or he could do something that would change his country's story for a very long time. Today the road leaves China and turns east, to Korea.
screen: `A MONK FROM CHINA.` → `IMAGES AND SCRIPTURES.` → `THE ROAD TURNS EAST.`

segments.voice: Korea was then three kingdoms: Goguryeo in the north, Baekje in the southwest, Silla in the southeast. The old Korean history called the Samguk Sagi records that in 372 a Chinese ruler sent the monk Sundo to Goguryeo with images and scriptures, and that King Sosurim received him. Within a few years, the same history says, temples were built for monks to live in. The welcome wasn't the same everywhere. Baekje, the history says, welcomed a foreign monk too, the teaching spread there, and from Baekje it would later travel on across the sea. Silla held out longer. A Korean collection of stories called the Samguk Yusa tells of Ichadon, a young official at the Silla court. The king wanted to honor the Buddha's teaching; his nobles refused. Ichadon offered to take the blame and be put to death. The story says that when he was executed, his blood ran white like milk, and the frightened court stopped resisting. Whatever readers make of the milk, Korean Buddhist tradition remembers him as the one who opened the door in Silla. A teaching doesn't land like a parcel. It comes in a monk's bag, gets a hearing at a court, meets suspicion, and slowly takes on the shape of the people who receive it. In the days ahead, Korea will give it its own thinkers, its own debates, and one very large library.

920.title: Wonhyo's skull
920.hook: Wonhyo drinks sweet water in the dark and in the morning sees it was in a skull: all is mind
920.carry: it was sweet in the dark
920.howItsDone: Korean Buddhists tell the story of Wonhyo's night in the tomb as a teaching on mind, and Wonhyo is honored in Korea as a great teacher and writer of commentaries.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Korea, where a monk arrived with scriptures and Ichadon opened the door in Silla. Your line: the teaching arrives.

Two Korean monks, no longer young, are on the road to China to study. Night falls in a storm. They find shelter in what feels like a cave and lie down, soaked and tired. In the dark, one of them, Wonhyo, wakes up desperately thirsty. He feels around, finds a vessel full of rainwater, and drinks. It's cool, and it tastes sweet. He sleeps content. In the morning light he sees what he drank from: a human skull. The shelter is a tomb. His stomach turns. And then something else happens.
screen: `A STORM ON THE ROAD TO CHINA.` → `SWEET WATER IN THE DARK.` → `MORNING: A SKULL.`

segments.voice: Wonhyo is sick at the sight, and right in the middle of the sickness he sees it. Nothing about the water changed overnight. Last night it was sweet; this morning it's revolting. Only his mind changed. The story gives him words like these: when a thought arises, all kinds of things arise; when the thought stops, a cave and a tomb are not two. It isn't a new idea he cooked up in a tomb. At Nalanda, some days back, this path sat with the first verse of the Dhammapada: all that we are comes from what we have thought. And the Mahayana sutras Wonhyo studied put it their own way: the three realms are mind only. Wonhyo had read those words. In the tomb he tasted them. The story is told more than one way. One early Chinese telling, in a collection of the lives of monks, has the two friends sleep in what they thought was an earthen shelter and wake to find it was an old tomb, with no skull and no water. The skull and the sweet drink come in later tellings, the version often told in Korea today. Either way, the point is the same: much of what makes a moment sweet or foul isn't in the thing. It's in the label stuck on it a second later. A message from a name you dread. A stain that turns out to be paint. The water hadn't changed. Wonhyo had.
screen: `THE WATER DIDN'T CHANGE.` · `THE THREE REALMS ARE MIND ONLY.` · `A TOMB IN THE OLDER TELLING.` · `THE LABEL COMES A SECOND LATER.` · then, large: `IT WAS SWEET IN THE DARK.`

921.title: Uisang goes on
921.hook: Wonhyo turns back; his friend Uisang goes on to China and brings back Huayan
921.howItsDone: Korean Buddhists honor Uisang as the founder of Hwaeom (Huayan) in Korea, and his seal-shaped poem on the Dharma realm is still recited and studied in Korean temples.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Wonhyo's skull, the same water sweet at night and foul in the morning. Your line: it was sweet in the dark.

Morning, outside the tomb. Two friends stand on the road with their bundles. One of them has just had the night of his life. Wonhyo says he doesn't need to go to China anymore: if the mind makes everything, there's nothing over there he can't find right here. He turns around and walks home. The other friend, Uisang, listens, nods, and picks up his bundle. He keeps walking toward the sea. No quarrel. No one is called wrong.
screen: `ONE TURNS BACK.` → `ONE PICKS UP HIS BUNDLE.` → `NO QUARREL.`

segments.voice: Uisang crossed to China and studied with the teacher Zhiyan, in the school called Huayan, named for the Flower Garland Sutra. That name came up earlier, on the list of Chinese schools. Huayan pictures the universe as a net of jewels, where every jewel reflects every other one. Nothing stands alone; each thing holds the whole. Uisang packed that teaching into a short poem, written in a winding pattern like a seal, so the reader's eye follows a path that folds back on itself. One line says, in plain terms, in one is all, and in many is one. Back in Korea he founded temples and taught students, and Huayan, called Hwaeom in Korean, took root. An old Chinese life of Uisang adds a story. Shanmiao, Seonmyo in Korean, was a young woman in China who loved him. When he sailed home, she leapt into the sea and became a dragon to guard his ship, and later a great rock to protect his temple. Wonhyo never went to China. He stayed, wrote commentaries, and later, the stories say, left the monk's life to walk among villagers, singing and teaching them the Buddha's name. One friend took the long road out; one took the short road in. Korean Buddhist tradition honors both. There's an echo of Huayan in that: two very different paths, each holding something of the other.
screen: `UISANG STUDIES HUAYAN IN CHINA.` · `A NET OF JEWELS, A SEAL-SHAPED POEM.` · `SEONMYO GUARDS HIS SHIP.` · `WONHYO SINGS IN THE VILLAGES.` · then, large: `TWO FRIENDS, TWO PATHS.`

922.title: Sudden and gradual
922.hook: Chinul: awaken suddenly, then cultivate gradually
922.howItsDone: In Korean Seon, Chinul's teaching of sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation is studied in monasteries, and his short works, such as Secrets on Cultivating the Mind, are read by monks and lay practitioners.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uisang carried Huayan home, Wonhyo stayed, and no one was called wrong. Your line: two friends, two paths.

A frozen pond in winter. One glance tells you the whole thing is water. Not partly. All of it. And yet you can't drink it, swim in it, or wash your hands in it. Knowing it's water doesn't melt it. That takes days of sun. A Korean monk named Chinul used that pond to answer an argument that had run through Chan for a long time, the one from the wall where two verses were written.
screen: `A FROZEN POND.` → `ALL OF IT IS WATER.` → `KNOWING DOESN'T MELT IT.`

segments.voice: Some days back, two verses went up on a monastery wall. One said the mind is a mirror that must be wiped clean, again and again. Huineng's answer said there is no mirror for dust to land on. People came to sum up the two sides as gradual and sudden: is awakening built up step by step, or seen all at once? Chinul was a Korean monk of the Goryeo kingdom who trained and taught in Korea. In a short work called Secrets on Cultivating the Mind, he says: both, in order. First you awaken suddenly. You see, all at once, that your own mind is already the Buddha-nature, the way you see that ice is water. Then you cultivate gradually. Old habits are still frozen in place, and they take time and steady practice to thaw. He gives another picture. A newborn baby, Chinul writes, has all the senses and limbs of a grown person, nothing missing, but it takes years before that strength is fully grown. Awakening is like being born. Practice is like growing up. Insight tends to arrive in a flash: in a conversation, on a walk, at a funeral. It's tempting to think the flash is the finish. Chinul says the flash is the start. The seeing is real, and the thaw still has to happen. Korean Seon, Korea's Chan, still looks back to Chinul as one of its great teachers.
screen: `THE MIRROR AND NO MIRROR.` · `FIRST AWAKEN, THEN CULTIVATE.` · `A NEWBORN STILL HAS TO GROW.` · `THE FLASH IS THE START.` · then, large: `SUDDEN, THEN SLOWLY.`

923.title: Eighty thousand woodblocks
923.hook: after invaders burn the first set, Korea carves the whole canon again in wood: the Tripitaka Koreana
923.howItsDone: The Tripitaka Koreana is kept at Haeinsa temple in Korea, where monks care for the blocks, and visitors come to see the halls that hold them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chinul's frozen pond. See it's water at once, then let it thaw. Your line: sudden, then slowly.

A carver bends over a block of wood. On it, written backward so it will print the right way round, are the characters of a Buddhist scripture. He cuts away everything that isn't a letter. One slip of the knife and a word is gone. Around him, more blocks wait, and more after those, enough to fill a library. This is Korea under the Goryeo kings, and the reason for all this patient cutting is a fire.
screen: `A CARVER, A KNIFE, A BLOCK.` → `LETTERS CUT BACKWARD.` → `THE REASON IS A FIRE.`

segments.voice: Goryeo had already carved the Buddhist canon once, the Tripitaka, the three baskets of teaching. Then Mongol armies invaded, and that first set of blocks was burned. The court and the monks decided to carve the whole canon again. A prayer written for the work by the scholar Yi Gyubo asks the Buddhas and protectors to look on the effort and turn the invaders back. So the carving was scholarship and devotion at once: every block a page of scripture, and the whole a vow. The texts were compared and corrected against other editions before the cutting began. Tradition says the carvers bowed after each character. In Korea the collection is known as the Palman Daejanggyeong, the Eighty Thousand Tripitaka, after its blocks. Today they are kept at Haeinsa, a temple in the mountains, in long wooden halls built with slatted windows to let the air move through. A burned set taught them that words can be lost. Their answer wasn't despair, and it wasn't speed. It was slowness, done right. Some things are made to be used up today. Others are made to outlast the people who made them. The carvers of Goryeo chose the second kind, one letter at a time.
screen: `THE FIRST SET BURNED.` · `CARVED AGAIN AS A VOW.` · `A BOW, TRADITION SAYS, FOR EACH CHARACTER.` · `KEPT AT HAEINSA.` · then, large: `CARVED TO LAST.`

chat.says: Why would anyone carve a whole library of scripture in wood twice?
options: A Mongol invasion burned the first set, so they carved it all again, as a vow.
The first set was full of errors, so the king had it all thrown out.
Paper was forbidden in Korea then, so wood was the only way to write.
chat.meaning: Mongol armies burned Goryeo's first set of blocks. Court and monks carved the canon again, checked and corrected, as scholarship and a vow.

924.title: Japan
924.hook: a Korean king sends a bronze Buddha across the sea; a divided court, and then Prince Shotoku
924.howItsDone: Japanese Buddhists honor Prince Shotoku as an early patron of the teaching, and temples linked to him, such as Horyuji near Nara, are still places of worship and pilgrimage.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Tripitaka Koreana, the canon carved again after the fire. Your line: carved to last.

A ship crosses the strait from Korea. On board, wrapped for the journey, is a Buddha of gilt bronze, with banners, canopies and rolls of scripture. It's a gift from the king of Baekje, one of the Korean kingdoms from a few days ago, to the ruler of Japan. With it comes a letter praising the teaching as hard to grasp and wonderful beyond measure. The ruler opens the gift, looks at the shining face, and does what rulers do with something new and powerful. He asks his ministers.
screen: `A GILT BRONZE BUDDHA.` → `A GIFT FROM BAEKJE.` → `THE RULER ASKS HIS MINISTERS.`

segments.voice: Japan's old chronicle, the Nihon Shoki, tells this story in the reign of Emperor Kinmei. The image and scriptures came from Baekje, so the teaching reached Japan by way of Korea. The chronicle says the ministers split. The Soga clan said the neighbors honor this Buddha, so should we. The Mononobe and Nakatomi clans said the land's own gods would be angered. Kinmei handed the image to the Soga chief to honor at his house, as a trial. Then sickness swept the country, the opponents blamed the foreign Buddha, and the image was thrown into a canal. Later, the chronicle tells of a regent, Prince Shotoku, who studied the sutras with teachers from Korea and gave the teaching a home at court. It credits him with seventeen guiding articles for officials. The first asks for harmony. The second asks that the three treasures be sincerely revered: the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha. Tradition links him to the founding of temples, among them Horyuji, near Nara, and Japanese Buddhists honor him as a founding patron. Look back at the week: Guanyin hearing the cries in China, Korea receiving a monk with scriptures, Wonhyo's sweet water, Uisang walking on, Chinul's frozen pond, the woodblocks, and now a bronze Buddha crossing the sea. Again and again, the teaching arrived from somewhere else, met doubt or hardship, and found people to carry it.
screen: `A GIFT FROM BAEKJE.` · `A COURT DIVIDED.` · `SHOTOKU REVERES THE THREE TREASURES.` · `A WEEK OF ARRIVALS.` · then, large: `THE TEACHING ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Picture the strait between the Korean peninsula and the islands of Japan, and follow one small boat across with its shining cargo. Then go inland to Nara, among low hills, where tomorrow's story waits, and rest there with the water still moving in your mind.
Japan. Where, the old chronicle says, a gilt bronze Buddha arrived as a gift from Korea, a court argued over it, and Prince Shotoku asked that the three treasures be revered.
Your line: the teaching arrives. Even a Buddha thrown into a canal didn't end the story. That's the week.

screen: `DAY 924 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE GREAT BUDDHA OF NARA.`

chat.says: Was Buddhism welcomed right away when it reached Japan?
options: Not at first: the court split, and after a sickness the image went in a canal.
Yes. The whole court agreed at once and built temples the same year.
It came straight from India by sea, so no one at court objected.
chat.meaning: The Nihon Shoki says the ministers split over Baekje's gift and opponents blamed it for a sickness. Later Prince Shotoku gave it a home at court.
